lead: This unit explains how a wire carrying a changing current becomes a radiator, how that radiator is described by a small set of numbers, and how those numbers predict the power that reaches a receiver. After it you can compute a pattern, a directivity, a radiation resistance, an efficiency, a near-field boundary and a complete link budget, and you can say why an antenna works the same way in transmit and receive.
about: The unit starts at the source. Chapter 2.1 shows that an accelerated charge radiates, builds the retarded potentials and solves the infinitesimal dipole. Chapter 2.2 turns its field into the vocabulary of patterns: lobes, beamwidth, beam solid angle, directivity and gain. Chapter 2.3 converts radiated power into a radiation resistance, adds loss for efficiency, and introduces effective aperture and polarization. Chapter 2.4 marks the distance beyond which all of these far-field formulas are valid. Chapters 2.5 and 2.6 apply the machinery to the two workhorse radiators, the half-wave dipole with its monopole and folded versions, and the small loop. Chapter 2.7 reverses the direction and uses reciprocity to treat the antenna as a receiver. Chapter 2.8 collects everything into the Friis equation and a decibel link budget.

chapters.idea: A charge moving at constant speed carries a field, but only an accelerating charge launches a field that keeps travelling after the charge has gone; that outgoing 1/r part is radiation.
chapters.depth: Start from the failure of static thinking: a steady current in a straight wire produces no radiation. Introduce retarded potentials. The magnetic vector potential A comes from the current density J, evaluated at the retarded time t − r/c, so the field at distance r shows what the current was doing r/c seconds ago. The electric vector potential F comes from a magnetic current density M. Some syllabi call the whole approach potential theory, and a few treat the general solution for an arbitrary current distribution through the Helmholtz integral and the F potential; only a few universities teach that part, so keep it to the statement of the integral and one line on why it exists. Then solve the infinitesimal dipole: a straight current element of length l much smaller than λ, carrying a uniform current I₀. Write the three field terms that fall as 1/r³, 1/r² and 1/r, and name only the 1/r term the radiation field. Give the far field as Eθ = j η β I₀ l sin θ e^(−jβr) / (4πr) and Hφ = Eθ/η. Define η = 120π ≈ 377 Ω (intrinsic impedance of free space), β = 2π/λ (phase constant, rad/m), r in metres, I₀ in amperes peak. Point out the sin θ pattern and the null along the wire axis. Mention the practical uses: the element is the building block for every wire antenna, and the same 1/r idea explains why a phone antenna must be a fair fraction of a wavelength.

chapters.example: A Hertzian dipole of length l = 1 cm carries a peak current I₀ = 1 A at 1 GHz. Find l/λ, the radiation resistance, the radiated power, and the far-field magnitude at 100 m broadside. Solution: λ = c/f = 0.3 m, so l/λ = 0.0333. R_r = 80π²(l/λ)² = 80 × 9.87 × 0.00111 = 0.877 Ω. P_rad = ½ I₀² R_r = 0.5 × 1 × 0.877 = 0.44 W. Broadside (θ = 90°, sin θ = 1): Eθ = η β I₀ l / (4πr) = 377 × 20.94 × 1 × 0.01 / (4π × 100) = 0.063 V/m. Check with power density: S = E²/(2η) = 5.2 µW/m², and P_rad D/(4πr²) with D = 1.5 gives the same 5.2 µW/m².
chapters.trap: Adding the 1/r² and 1/r³ terms into the far field, and forgetting sin θ (the field is zero along the wire axis, not maximum). Also mixing the element length l in metres with the wavelength, and using rms current in one place and peak current in another.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: Maxwell's equations, the wave equation, and the idea of a retarded solution.
chapters.leave: Radiation resistance and efficiency to Chapter 2.3; the near-field boundary to Chapter 2.4; the loop version of the same derivation to Chapter 2.6.

chapters.idea: An antenna pattern is a shape, and directivity, gain and beamwidth are the few numbers that reduce that shape to something a link budget can use.
chapters.depth: Define the radiation pattern as the far-field strength against angle, drawn as a field pattern or a power pattern, and usually in dB. Name the lobes: main, side, back, and the nulls between them. Define radiation intensity U(θ, φ) = r² S in W/sr, which removes the spreading. Normalise it to P_n(θ, φ). Define the beam solid angle Ω_A = ∬ P_n dΩ in steradians, then directivity D = 4π/Ω_A, which compares the antenna with an isotropic radiator that has D = 1. Define gain G = η_rad D, and say clearly that gain includes losses while directivity does not. Express both in dBi: value in dBi = 10 log₁₀(value). Define HPBW (half-power or −3 dB beamwidth) and FNBW (first-null beamwidth), and give the rough estimate D ≈ 41253/(θ_E θ_H) with both angles in degrees for a pencil beam. Add the terms some syllabi list here: isotropic, omnidirectional and directional as a three-way classification, and return loss = −20 log₁₀|Γ| with Γ the reflection coefficient at the antenna input (VSWR itself is in Unit 1).

figure.aria: Two curves against angle: the field pattern sin θ and the power pattern sin squared θ, whose half-power points fall at 45 and 135 degrees.

chapters.example: An antenna has a field pattern F(θ) = sin θ with no φ dependence. Find the HPBW, the beam solid angle, the directivity and the gain, taking radiation efficiency 0.9. Solution: half power means sin²θ = 0.5, so θ = 45° and 135°; HPBW = 135° − 45° = 90°. Ω_A = 2π ∫₀^π sin³θ dθ = 2π × 4/3 = 8.38 sr. D = 4π/Ω_A = 12.57/8.38 = 1.5, that is 10 log₁₀1.5 = 1.76 dBi. G = 0.9 × 1.5 = 1.35, that is 1.30 dBi.
chapters.trap: Reading the half-power points off the field pattern instead of the power pattern (it moves the answer to 60° instead of 45°). Quoting gain when the question asks for directivity, and forgetting that a lossless antenna has G = D.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for the far-field expression that produces the pattern.
chapters.leave: Pattern multiplication and array factors to Unit 3; S-parameters and return-loss measurement to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Radiation resistance converts radiated power into an equivalent resistor, efficiency says how much of the input power actually escapes, and effective aperture says how much of an incoming wave the antenna can capture.
chapters.depth: Define R_r by P_rad = ½|I|² R_r, with I the current at a stated reference point — this reference matters and must be said every time. Give the short-dipole result R_r = 80π²(l/λ)², the half-wave dipole 73 Ω and the quarter-wave monopole 36.5 Ω. Add loss resistance R_L for conductor and dielectric loss, define radiation efficiency η_rad = R_r/(R_r + R_L), and note G = η_rad D. Define effective aperture A_e through P_r = S A_e with S the incident power density in W/m², give the universal relation A_e = D λ²/(4π) valid for any antenna, and define aperture efficiency for antennas with a physical area, e_ap = A_e/A_phys. Handle polarization: linear, circular and elliptical; axial ratio; circular polarization from two crossed dipoles fed 90° apart; the polarization loss factor PLF = |ρ̂_w · ρ̂_a|², which is 1 when matched, 0.5 (3 dB loss) for linear against circular, and 0 when crossed.

figure.title: Radiation resistance in ohms
figure.aria: A table of radiation resistance rising from a fraction of an ohm for very short dipoles to 73 ohms for a half-wave dipole.

chapters.example: A short dipole has length l = λ/20 and a loss resistance R_L = 0.5 Ω. Find its radiation resistance, its radiation efficiency, and its effective aperture at 300 MHz, taking D = 1.5. Solution: R_r = 80π²(l/λ)² = 80 × 9.87 × (1/20)² = 1.97 Ω. η_rad = 1.97/(1.97 + 0.5) = 0.80, that is 80 per cent. At 300 MHz, λ = 1 m, so A_e = D λ²/(4π) = 1.5 × 1/(12.57) = 0.119 m².
chapters.trap: Quoting R_r without saying which current it refers to; a folded dipole has four times the input resistance for the same radiated power. A second trap is using A_e = λ²/4π for every antenna — that value is only for D = 1.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.1 and 2.2 for the far field and for directivity.
chapters.leave: Physical apertures of horns and dishes to Unit 3; noise temperature and noise figure to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: The formulas of this unit hold only far enough away, and the distance where the 1/r field wins is fixed by the antenna size and the wavelength.
chapters.depth: Split the space around an antenna into three regions and give the boundary of each. Reactive near field: r < 0.62√(D³/λ), where D is the largest antenna dimension in metres; here stored energy dominates and the wave impedance is not 377 Ω. Radiating near field (Fresnel): between that and the far field, where the pattern is still forming and the phase across the aperture is not flat. Far field (Fraunhofer): r > 2D²/λ, plus r much greater than D and r much greater than λ; here the pattern is independent of r and E/H = η. Derive the 2D²/λ rule from the allowed path difference across the aperture (a phase error of π/8, that is 22.5°, gives the constant 2). For an electrically small antenna the reactive region extends to about λ/2π and the 2D²/λ rule is meaningless, so the λ criteria take over. Give the applications: antenna pattern measurement distance, near-field probes, NFC and RFID coupling, and specific absorption rate checks on handsets.

chapters.example: A horn has largest dimension D = 1 m. Find the outer edge of its reactive near field and the start of its far field at 300 MHz and at 100 MHz. Solution: the reactive edge is 0.62√(D³/λ). At 300 MHz, λ = 1 m, so it is 0.62 m. Far field needs r > 2D²/λ = 2 m and r > 1.6λ = 1.6 m, so r > 2 m. At 100 MHz, λ = 3 m, 2D²/λ = 0.67 m but 1.6λ = 4.8 m, and the λ criterion wins, so the far field starts at about 4.8 m.
chapters.trap: Applying 2D²/λ to a small antenna, where it gives a distance shorter than a wavelength. The other slip is reading D in the formula as directivity when it means the largest physical dimension in metres.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for the 1/r, 1/r² and 1/r³ field terms.
chapters.leave: Measurement ranges and anechoic chambers to Unit 3; exposure and SAR limits to a specialised course.

chapters.idea: The half-wave dipole is a resonant antenna that matches itself to a feed line, the monopole is its half above a ground plane, and the folded dipole multiplies its input resistance by about four.
chapters.depth: Draw the sinusoidal current distribution on a half-wave dipole: zero at the tips, maximum at the centre, following cos(βz). State the input impedance of an exact λ/2 dipole as 73 + j42.5 Ω, and that shortening to about 0.47λ cancels the reactance and gives about 73 Ω resistive — this is why practical dipoles are cut short. Give R_r = 73 Ω and D = 1.64 (2.15 dBi), with the pattern factor cos(π/2 cos θ)/sin θ. Cover the quarter-wave monopole above a ground plane by image theory: half the dipole, Z_in ≈ 36.5 Ω, D = 3.28 (5.15 dBi) because the power goes into a half space only, same pattern above the ground. Cover the folded dipole: two parallel half-wave conductors joined at the ends, current splits equally, input resistance about four times, roughly 300 Ω, which suits 300 Ω twin line; bandwidth is wider. Define a balun in one line as the transition from a balanced dipole to an unbalanced coaxial feed.

figure.aria: Current along a half-wave dipole as a cosine that is maximum at the centre and zero at the tips, compared with the triangular current of a short dipole.

chapters.example: A half-wave dipole is cut to 0.47λ for 100 MHz and its current maximum is 1 A. Find its length, the radiated power, the broadside field at 1 km, and the power density there. Solution: λ = 3 m, so l = 0.47 × 3 = 1.41 m. P_rad = ½ I₀² R_r = 0.5 × 1 × 73 = 36.5 W. Broadside field E = η I₀/(2πr) = 60 I₀/r = 60 × 1/1000 = 0.06 V/m. Power density S = E²/(2η) = 0.0036/754 = 4.8 µW/m². Cross-check: P_rad D/(4πr²) = 36.5 × 1.64/(12.57 × 10⁶) = 4.8 µW/m².
chapters.trap: Using D = 1.5 for a half-wave dipole; that value belongs to the short dipole. Two more: forgetting the 0.47 shortening and claiming a pure 73 Ω, and giving a monopole 2.15 dBi when its directivity doubles to 3.28 because no power goes below the ground plane.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3 for the dipole field, directivity and radiation resistance.
chapters.leave: Yagi-Uda, log-periodic and array designs to Unit 3; balun and matching hardware to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: A loop much smaller than a wavelength behaves as a magnetic dipole: the same doughnut pattern as a short dipole, but a radiation resistance so small that loss usually wins.
chapters.depth: Define a small loop as one whose circumference is under about λ/10, so the current is nearly uniform around it. Define the magnetic moment m = N I A, with N the number of turns, I the current in amperes and A the loop area in m². State that the far field has Eφ and Hθ with a sin θ pattern — the electric and magnetic roles are swapped compared with the short dipole. Give R_r = 320π⁴(NA/λ²)², which for a single turn becomes R_r = 20π²(C/λ)⁴ with C the circumference. Show that R_r grows as the fourth power of size, which is why small loops are so inefficient. Give the practical face of the loop: the ferrite rod antenna in a medium-wave radio, where a ferrite core multiplies the effective area, and the direction-finding loop with nulls along its axis. Note that the loop null is sharp, which is useful for finding a bearing.

chapters.example: A small loop has N = 10 turns of radius a = 0.1 m and works at 10 MHz. Its loss resistance is 0.05 Ω. Find the loop area, the radiation resistance and the radiation efficiency. Solution: A = πa² = π × 0.01 = 0.0314 m². λ = 30 m. NA/λ² = 10 × 0.0314/900 = 3.49 × 10⁻⁴. R_r = 320π⁴(NA/λ²)² = 31171 × (3.49 × 10⁻⁴)² = 3.8 × 10⁻³ Ω, that is 3.8 mΩ. η_rad = 0.0038/(0.0038 + 0.05) = 0.07, about 7 per cent. This is why a small loop needs many turns and a low-loss conductor.
chapters.trap: Squaring only the area and dropping N, so the answer is too small by N². Also using the wire radius where the loop radius belongs, and using the diameter as the radius inside A = πa².
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.1 and 2.3 for the dipole derivation and for radiation resistance and efficiency.
chapters.leave: The loop as a receiver to Chapter 2.7; ferrite materials and circulators to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: The same piece of metal that radiates is also a good receiver, and reciprocity guarantees that its pattern, impedance and gain are identical in both roles.
chapters.depth: Model the receiving antenna as a Thevenin source: an open-circuit voltage V_oc induced by the incoming field, in series with the antenna impedance Z_a = R_r + R_L + jX_a. Define effective length l_eff by V_oc = E l_eff cos ψ, with ψ the angle between the field and the antenna, giving l_eff = l for a short dipole and l_eff = λ/π for a half-wave dipole. Deliver maximum power with a conjugate match, Z_L = Z_a*, and state that under this match half the captured power goes to the load and half is re-radiated or scattered by R_r. Write the received power as P_r = S A_e with A_e = D λ²/4π. State the reciprocity theorem: the transmit and receive patterns are identical, and the impedance is the same in both directions, so one set of measurements is enough. Add the polarization match factor to the received power, P_r = S A_e PLF, with PLF defined in Chapter 2.3.

messages.label: field E at the same r

figure.aria: A two-way timeline showing that driving antenna A and receiving on B, then swapping the roles, gives the same received power, which is reciprocity.

chapters.example: A short dipole of directivity 1.5 receives a wave at 100 MHz with power density S = 10 µW/m², polarization matched. Find its effective aperture and the power delivered to a matched load, in watts and dBm. Solution: λ = c/f = 3 m. A_e = D λ²/(4π) = 1.5 × 9/12.57 = 1.07 m². P_r = S A_e = 10 × 10⁻⁶ × 1.07 = 10.7 µW. In dBm: 10 log₁₀(10.7 × 10⁻³) = −19.7 dBm.
chapters.trap: Treating A_e as the physical area of a wire antenna; it is a capture area that can be far larger than the metal. Also assuming all the captured power reaches the load, when under a conjugate match half is scattered, and ignoring the polarization loss factor.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.2 and 2.3 for directivity and effective aperture.
chapters.leave: Noise floor, sensitivity and noise figure to Unit 5; gain and pattern measurement to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Friis multiplies the transmit power by both antenna gains and divides by the spreading loss of free space, and in decibels that becomes a simple sum called a link budget.
chapters.depth: Derive it in three lines: power density at the receiver S = P_t G_t/(4πd²), received power P_r = S A_e with A_e = G_r λ²/(4π), so P_r = P_t G_t G_r (λ/4πd)². Define every symbol with its unit. Name (4πd/λ)² the free-space path loss, FSPL, and write it in dB as 20 log₁₀(4πd/λ) = 32.44 + 20 log₁₀(f in MHz) + 20 log₁₀(d in km). Build the decibel budget: P_r(dBm) = P_t(dBm) + G_t(dBi) + G_r(dBi) − FSPL(dB) − L_misc(dB), where L_misc covers cable, connector and mismatch loss. Define EIRP = P_t G_t in dBm and note the regulator's limit on it. Define link margin = P_r − receiver sensitivity, and say that a positive margin is a working link. State the assumptions: far-field distance, matched polarization, no obstructions, no multipath, no atmospheric loss; those belong to propagation.

figure.aria: Received-to-transmitted power ratio in decibels against distance for 2.4 and 5 GHz, with the higher frequency curve always lower by about 6 dB.

chapters.example: A 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi link has P_t = 100 mW, G_t = G_r = 1 (0 dBi), distance d = 100 m, cable and connector loss 2 dB, and receiver sensitivity −90 dBm. Find λ, the free-space path loss, the received power and the link margin. Solution: λ = c/f = 0.125 m. FSPL = 20 log₁₀(4πd/λ) = 20 log₁₀(4π × 100/0.125) = 20 log₁₀(10053) = 80.0 dB. P_t = 100 mW = 20 dBm. P_r = 20 + 0 + 0 − 80.0 − 2 = −62 dBm. Margin = −62 − (−90) = 28 dB.
chapters.trap: Dropping one of the two gains, or mixing units: d must be in the same length unit as λ, so d in kilometres with λ in metres gives a nonsense answer. Also treating FSPL as the only loss and forgetting cable, mismatch and polarization.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.2, 2.3 and 2.7 for gain, effective aperture and the receiving antenna.
chapters.leave: Noise figure, sensitivity and cascaded blocks to Unit 5; ground reflection, diffraction and path-loss models to Unit 3.
